title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats

Title:Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

report.summary: Paper shows selective MXFP6 and MXFP8 quantization on AMD MI350X speeds production recommendation/ranking inference 1.5–14.3% end-to-end while meeting strict 0.01% NE parity.
report.background: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, especially in digital advertising, must serve massive inference throughput while remaining extremely sensitive to precision loss. Unlike many LLMs that tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production R&R systems often enforce a launch bar of 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) relative to an FP16 or FP32 baseline. That tight constraint has historically blocked aggressive low-precision deployment. Microscaling (MX) formats offer block-scaled FP8 and FP6 arithmetic, promising lower memory traffic and faster matrix multiplication. This paper evaluates MXFP8 and MXFP6 on AMD MI350X for industrial-scale R&R inference, testing whether selective low-precision application can deliver real speedups without breaching production accuracy thresholds.
key_points: The paper targets R&R models’ unusually strict accuracy bar: quality must stay within 0.01% NE of an FP16/FP32 baseline. Instead of quantizing everything aggressively, it selectively applies MXFP6 only where the accuracy budget allows, preserving parity while still capturing throughput gains.

MXFP8 is presented as a viable alternative to row-wise FP8. The two formats show nearly identical accuracy on the tested models, so engineers can choose the faster kernel for each GEMM shape. Across supported linear layers, MXFP8 delivers 1.33–1.55x GEMM kernel speedups over FP16.

The headline result is native MXFP6 GEMM: weights and activations are quantized and computed directly on 6-bit elements. The authors report 1.73–1.99x speedups over FP16 across linear layers and up to 2.90x on individual layers, which they describe as the first significant native MXFP6 GEMM speedup in R&R and LLM domains.

End-to-end gains from selective MXFP6 are meaningful in production terms: 1.5–5.3% higher inference throughput for Model A and 7.6–14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations. The results suggest low-precision formats can improve serving economics without violating strict NE thresholds.

The study is tied to AMD MI350X and industrial-scale ads ranking workloads. It highlights layer-wise selectivity and kernel-shape autotuning as practical techniques for adopting MX formats in latency-sensitive, quality-critical recommendation systems rather than treating quantization as a single global setting.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the work signals that low-precision inference is moving beyond FP8 toward block-scaled 6-bit formats, with hardware and software co-design enabling measurable production gains. For developers, it reinforces selective, layer-aware quantization and per-shape kernel selection as practical tactics: not every layer needs the same precision, and accuracy budgets should be measured end-to-end. For regular users, the benefits are indirect but real—faster, cheaper recommendation and ads serving can mean more responsive feeds and lower infrastructure costs. The main caveat is portability: results are specific to AMD MI350X and the tested R&R models, so teams must revalidate NE margins and kernel support on their own stacks before deploying MXFP6 broadly.
report.tools: Follow AMD Quark and ROCm for MXFP8/MXFP6 quantization and kernel support on MI350X-class hardware; the Open Compute Project Microscaling (MX) specification for format details; and production recommendation inference stacks such as TorchRec-style frameworks for layer-wise quantization experiments. Also watch FP8/MX GEMM kernel libraries and autotuning tools that let teams compare row-wise FP8 versus MXFP8 per GEMM shape.
